title: The d-th syzygy of a module of projective dimension at most d is projective
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $M$ an $R$-module and $d\ge0$ an integer such that $M$ has a projective resolution of length $\le d$ [def-weil-pbc-finite-global-dimension]. Let $e\ge d-1$ and let $F_e\to F_{e-1}\to\dots\to F_0\to M\to0$ be an exact sequence [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence] of $R$-modules with every $F_i$ projective [def-weil-pbc-projective-module]. Then $\operatorname{Ker}(F_e\to F_{e-1})$ (for $e=0$: $\operatorname{Ker}(F_0\to M)$) is a projective $R$-module. In particular (taking $e=d-1$ when $d\ge1$): if $0\to K\to F_{d-1}\to\dots\to F_0\to M\to0$ is exact with all $F_i$ projective, then $K$ is projective; and if $d=0$, $M$ itself is projective.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00O5 (lemma-independent-resolution, line 26585) and its proof (induction on d using Schanuel's Lemma Tag 00O3, lemma-Schanuel). Tag verified in tags/tags: 00O5,algebra-lemma-independent-resolution

proof.text: (Notation and the inductive claim.) For an exact sequence $F_e\xrightarrow{\partial_e}F_{e-1}\to\dots\xrightarrow{\partial_1}F_0\xrightarrow{\partial_0}M\to0$ exactness [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence] means: $\partial_0$ is surjective and $\mathrm{Im}(\partial_{i+1})=\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_i)$ for $0\le i\le e-1$; the module to be shown projective is $\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_e)$ (for $e=0$ this is $\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_0)=\mathrm{Ker}(F_0\to M)$). For an integer $d\ge0$ let $C(d)$ be the claim: for every $R$-module $M$ that has a projective resolution of length $\le d$ [def-weil-pbc-finite-global-dimension], every integer $e\ge\max(0,d-1)$ and every exact sequence $F_e\to\dots\to F_0\to M\to0$ with all $F_i$ projective, $\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_e)$ is projective. The first assertion of the lemma is $C(d)$ for all $d$; we prove $C(d)$ by induction on $d$ (Steps 2-3 for $d=0$, Steps 4-8 for $d\ge1$ assuming $C(d-1)$). The source states the lemma for $M$ of projective dimension exactly $d$ and applies the induction hypothesis to a module with a resolution of length $d-1$; the claim with 'length $\le d$' is the form in which that induction is valid as written.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00O5 (lemma-independent-resolution), lines 26594-26627

proof.text: (Case $d=0$: $M$ is projective.) A projective resolution of length $\le0$ is an exact sequence $0\to P_0\xrightarrow{\delta_0}M\to0$ with $P_0$ projective [def-weil-pbc-finite-global-dimension]; exactness at $P_0$ and at $M$ say that $\delta_0$ is injective and surjective [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence], so $\delta_0:P_0\to M$ is an isomorphism and $M$ is projective by [lem-weil-pbc-projective-direct-summand] (2).

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00O5 (lemma-independent-resolution), lines 26594-26627

proof.text: (Case $d=0$, by induction on $e$.) Let $D(e)$ be the claim: for every projective $R$-module $M$ and every exact sequence $F_e\to\dots\to F_0\to M\to0$ with all $F_i$ projective, $\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_e)$ is projective. $D(0)$: put $K_0=\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_0)$; $0\to K_0\to F_0\xrightarrow{\partial_0}M\to0$ is short exact ($\partial_0$ surjective), $M$ is projective, so by [lem-weil-pbc-ses-projective-quotient-splits] there is $r:F_0\to K_0$ with $r\circ\mathrm{incl}=\mathrm{id}_{K_0}$ (the source's splitting $F_0=\mathrm{Ker}(F_0\to M)\oplus M$), and $K_0$ is projective by [lem-weil-pbc-projective-direct-summand] (1), $F_0$ being projective. $D(e-1)\Rightarrow D(e)$ for $e\ge1$ (the source's 'replacing $M$ by $\mathrm{Ker}(F_0\to M)$ we decrease $e$'): by $D(0)$ applied to $F_0\to M\to0$, $K_0$ is projective. Since $\mathrm{Im}(\partial_1)=K_0$, $\partial_1$ corestricts to a surjection $\partial_1':F_1\to K_0$ with $\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_1')=\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_1)$ ($K_0\subseteq F_0$). Hence $F_e\to\dots\to F_2\xrightarrow{\partial_2}F_1\xrightarrow{\partial'_1}K_0\to0$ is exact (at $K_0$: $\partial'_1$ surjective; at $F_1$, if $e\ge2$: $\mathrm{Ker}(\partial'_1)=\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_1)=\mathrm{Im}(\partial_2)$; at $F_i$, $2\le i\le e-1$: as before); with $F'_i=F_{i+1}$ it is an exact sequence $F'_{e-1}\to\dots\to F'_0\to K_0\to0$ of projective modules over the projective module $K_0$. By $D(e-1)$ the kernel of its last map is projective: for $e\ge2$ this is $\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_e)$; for $e=1$ it is $\mathrm{Ker}(\partial'_1)=\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_1)$. So $D(e)$ holds for all $e\ge0$, and with Step 2 this is $C(0)$ ($e\ge\max(0,-1)=0$).

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00O5 (lemma-independent-resolution), lines 26594-26627

proof.text: (Case $d\ge1$: Schanuel.) Let $d\ge1$, assume $C(d-1)$, and let $M$, $e\ge\max(0,d-1)$ and $F_e\to\dots\to F_0\to M\to0$ be as in $C(d)$. By [def-weil-pbc-finite-global-dimension] choose an exact sequence $0\to P_d\xrightarrow{\delta_d}P_{d-1}\to\dots\to P_1\xrightarrow{\delta_1}P_0\xrightarrow{\delta_0}M\to0$ with all $P_i$ projective (the source takes one of minimal length; any one of length $\le d$ serves). Put $K_0=\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_0)\subseteq F_0$ and $L_0=\mathrm{Ker}(\delta_0)\subseteq P_0$. Since $\partial_0$ and $\delta_0$ are surjective [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence], $0\to K_0\to F_0\xrightarrow{\partial_0}M\to0$ and $0\to L_0\to P_0\xrightarrow{\delta_0}M\to0$ are short exact with projective middle terms, and [lem-weil-pbc-schanuel] (with $K=K_0$, $P_1=F_0$, $L=L_0$, $P_2=P_0$) gives an isomorphism of $R$-modules $\varphi:K_0\oplus P_0\xrightarrow{\sim}L_0\oplus F_0$.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00O5 (lemma-independent-resolution), lines 26594-26627

proof.text: (Case $d\ge1$, $e=0$.) Then $0\ge d-1$, so $d=1$ and the resolution is $0\to P_1\xrightarrow{\delta_1}P_0\xrightarrow{\delta_0}M\to0$. Exactness at $P_1$ makes $\delta_1$ injective and exactness at $P_0$ gives $\mathrm{Im}(\delta_1)=L_0$ [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence], so $\delta_1$ induces an isomorphism $P_1\cong L_0$ and hence $P_1\oplus F_0\cong L_0\oplus F_0\cong K_0\oplus P_0$ (via $\varphi^{-1}$). $P_1\oplus F_0$ is projective by [lem-weil-pbc-projective-direct-sum], so $K_0\oplus P_0$ is projective by [lem-weil-pbc-projective-direct-summand] (2). The maps $i:K_0\to K_0\oplus P_0$, $k\mapsto(k,0)$, and $s:K_0\oplus P_0\to K_0$, $(k,x)\mapsto k$, satisfy $s\circ i=\mathrm{id}_{K_0}$, so $K_0=\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_0)=\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_e)$ is projective by [lem-weil-pbc-projective-direct-summand] (1).

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00O5 (lemma-independent-resolution), lines 26594-26627

proof.text: (Case $d\ge1$, $e\ge1$: a projective resolution of length $\le d-1$ of $N=K_0\oplus P_0$.) Put $Q_0=P_1\oplus F_0$ and $Q_i=P_{i+1}$ for $1\le i\le d-1$, with the maps $\varepsilon:Q_0\to L_0\oplus F_0$, $(x,y)\mapsto(\delta_1x,y)$ (well defined: $\delta_1x\in\mathrm{Im}(\delta_1)=L_0$), $\rho_1:Q_1=P_2\to Q_0$, $x\mapsto(\delta_2x,0)$ (if $d\ge2$), and $\rho_i=\delta_{i+1}:Q_i\to Q_{i-1}$ for $2\le i\le d-1$. The sequence $0\to Q_{d-1}\to\dots\to Q_1\xrightarrow{\rho_1}Q_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}L_0\oplus F_0\to0$ is exact [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence]: $\varepsilon$ is surjective since $\mathrm{Im}(\delta_1)=L_0$; $\mathrm{Ker}(\varepsilon)=\mathrm{Ker}(\delta_1)\oplus0$, which is $0$ if $d=1$ ($\delta_1$ injective by exactness of the resolution at $P_1$) and equals $\mathrm{Im}(\delta_2)\oplus0=\mathrm{Im}(\rho_1)$ if $d\ge2$; for $d\ge2$, $\mathrm{Ker}(\rho_1)=\mathrm{Ker}(\delta_2)$, which is $0$ if $d=2$ and $\mathrm{Im}(\delta_3)=\mathrm{Im}(\rho_2)$ if $d\ge3$; exactness at $Q_i$ for $2\le i\le d-1$ (including injectivity of $\rho_{d-1}=\delta_d$) is exactness of the resolution at $P_{i+1}$. $Q_0$ is projective by [lem-weil-pbc-projective-direct-sum] and $Q_i=P_{i+1}$ ($i\ge1$) is projective. Replacing $\varepsilon$ by $\varphi^{-1}\circ\varepsilon:Q_0\to N$ (Step 4) keeps the sequence exact (an isomorphism preserves surjectivity and $\mathrm{Ker}(\varphi^{-1}\circ\varepsilon)=\mathrm{Ker}(\varepsilon)$). So $0\to Q_{d-1}\to\dots\to Q_0\to N\to0$ is a projective resolution of $N=K_0\oplus P_0$ of length $\le d-1$ [def-weil-pbc-finite-global-dimension]; this is the source's resolution $0\to P_d\to\dots\to P_2\to P_1\oplus F_0\to\mathrm{Ker}(P_0\to M)\oplus F_0\to0$ transported along Schanuel's isomorphism.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00O5 (lemma-independent-resolution), lines 26594-26627

proof.text: (Case $d\ge1$, $e\ge1$: an exact sequence of length $e-1$ over $N$, and the induction hypothesis.) Put $G_0=F_1\oplus P_0$ and $G_i=F_{i+1}$ for $1\le i\le e-1$, with $\eta:G_0\to N=K_0\oplus P_0$, $(x,p)\mapsto(\partial_1x,p)$ (well defined: $\partial_1x\in\mathrm{Im}(\partial_1)=K_0$), $\sigma_1:G_1=F_2\to G_0$, $x\mapsto(\partial_2x,0)$ (if $e\ge2$), and $\sigma_i=\partial_{i+1}:G_i\to G_{i-1}$ for $2\le i\le e-1$. The sequence $G_{e-1}\to\dots\to G_1\xrightarrow{\sigma_1}G_0\xrightarrow{\eta}N\to0$ is exact [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence]: $\eta$ is surjective since $\mathrm{Im}(\partial_1)=K_0$; $\mathrm{Ker}(\eta)=\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_1)\oplus0$, which for $e\ge2$ is $\mathrm{Im}(\partial_2)\oplus0=\mathrm{Im}(\sigma_1)$; for $e\ge3$, $\mathrm{Ker}(\sigma_1)=\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_2)=\mathrm{Im}(\partial_3)=\mathrm{Im}(\sigma_2)$; exactness at $G_i$ for $2\le i\le e-2$ is exactness of $F_\bullet$ at $F_{i+1}$. $G_0$ is projective by [lem-weil-pbc-projective-direct-sum], and $G_i=F_{i+1}$ ($i\ge1$) is projective. Since $e\ge1$ and $e\ge d-1$, we have $e-1\ge\max(0,(d-1)-1)$; and $N$ has a projective resolution of length $\le d-1$ by Step 6. So $C(d-1)$ applies to $N$ and this sequence (the source's $F_e\to\dots\to F_2\to P_0\oplus F_1\to P_0\oplus\mathrm{Ker}(F_0\to M)\to0$): the kernel of its last map is projective, namely $\mathrm{Ker}(\sigma_{e-1})$ if $e\ge2$ and $\mathrm{Ker}(\eta)$ if $e=1$.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00O5 (lemma-independent-resolution), lines 26594-26627

proof.text: (Identification of the kernel; end of the induction.) If $e\ge3$, $\sigma_{e-1}=\partial_e$, so $\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_e)$ is projective by Step 7. If $e=2$, $\mathrm{Ker}(\sigma_1)=\{x\in F_2:(\partial_2x,0)=0\}=\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_2)$. If $e=1$, $\mathrm{Ker}(\eta)=\{(x,p)\in F_1\oplus P_0:\partial_1x=0,\ p=0\}=\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_1)\oplus0$, and $x\mapsto(x,0)$ is an isomorphism $\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_1)\cong\mathrm{Ker}(\eta)$, so $\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_1)$ is projective by [lem-weil-pbc-projective-direct-summand] (2) (the source writes this kernel as $\mathrm{Ker}(F_1\oplus P_0\to F_0\oplus P_0)$, which is the same submodule $\mathrm{Ker}(\partial_1)\oplus0$, and leaves the identification to the reader). With Step 5 for $e=0$ this proves $C(d)$, and by induction $C(d)$ holds for every $d\ge0$.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00O5 (lemma-independent-resolution), lines 26594-26627

proof.text: (The particular cases.) Let $d\ge1$ and let $0\to K\xrightarrow{j}F_{d-1}\to\dots\to F_0\to M\to0$ be exact with all $F_i$ projective. The part $F_{d-1}\to\dots\to F_0\to M\to0$ is exact, so by $C(d)$ with $e=d-1\ge\max(0,d-1)$ the module $Z=\mathrm{Ker}(F_{d-1}\to F_{d-2})$ ($Z=\mathrm{Ker}(F_0\to M)$ if $d=1$) is projective; exactness at $K$ and at $F_{d-1}$ [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence] say that $j$ is injective with image $Z$, so $j:K\to Z$ is an isomorphism and $K$ is projective by [lem-weil-pbc-projective-direct-summand] (2). If $d=0$, $M$ is projective by Step 2.
